prompt: When counting distinct substrings from sorted suffixes, why subtract every adjacent LCP value rather than just the largest one?

options.text: Only the longest repeated substring contributes any duplication.
options.explanation: Shorter repeated prefixes also represent duplicate substrings.

options.text: Each suffix can repeat prefixes already introduced by its sorted predecessor.
options.explanation: Correct. Every suffix contributes its new prefixes after excluding those shared ones.

options.text: LCP values count suffixes that should be deleted from the index.
options.explanation: Suffixes stay in the index; their shared prefixes are what must not be counted twice.

options.text: The largest LCP always equals the string length.
options.explanation: Adjacent distinct suffixes do not have to share any prefix.

workedExample: Every substring begins at some position and is a prefix of that suffix. In sorted suffix order, the prefixes shared with the preceding suffix have already been counted. Exclude those for each suffix; its longer prefixes are new. Using only the largest LCP misses duplication at other suffix boundaries.

prompt: A bioinformatics service holds a fixed 3-billion-character genome and answers millions of short pattern queries (about thirty characters). Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Running KMP per query costs O(n) each, scanning roughly three billion characters again for every query, where n is the text length
options.explanation: Correct. Linear-time matching scans the whole text for every query; millions of queries would be a character-visit scale in the quadrillions.

options.text: With a suffix array, all occurrences of a pattern form one contiguous range, found by binary search in O(m log n)
options.explanation: Correct. Sorted suffixes that start with p are adjacent. Halving 3 billion suffixes down to one takes about 32 steps, so each of two boundary searches takes about 32 comparisons of up to 30 characters.

options.text: A suffix tree is preferred because it uses less memory than a suffix array
options.explanation: A pointer-based suffix tree has representation-dependent node overhead. A suffix array is one integer per text position; claiming a universally smaller suffix tree is unjustified without measured representations. Compressed FM-indexes offer another trade-off.

options.text: Building the suffix array necessarily takes O(n²) time
options.explanation: Naive sorting can be that slow, but prefix doubling is O(n log n) with radix sort, and SA-IS or DC3 build it in O(n).

options.text: The one-off build cost is amortised over the many queries
options.explanation: Correct. Pre-processing the fixed text once is exactly the trade suffix arrays make, versus O(n) per query without an index.

workedExample: The text is fixed and queried repeatedly, so a one-off index can replace repeated full scans. Sorted suffixes beginning with the same pattern are contiguous; binary searches find their boundaries, then reporting hits adds output work. Build time, the packed index, text, auxiliary arrays and implementation overhead all need a memory budget. Suffix trees are not universally smaller. Linear construction also requires appropriate alphabet assumptions.
